analysis.one_liner: Bars federal courts from sealing court records or settlements that hide information about public dangers.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for over a year, got one subcommittee hearing in September 1992, and died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies accused of making dangerous products often settle lawsuits on condition that the evidence stay secret, so the next batch of customers never hears about the danger. This bill would stop federal courts from issuing secrecy orders and would void settlement clauses that conceal information about anything that has caused harm and is likely to again. Anyone affected — including reporters, who the bill says are automatically affected — could go to court to force the information out.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers who could learn about hazards before being hurt by them, and the news media and public-interest groups who could sue to unseal hidden evidence. Courts would still review disputed material privately first, so not everything would come out.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal courts from issuing protective orders that have the purpose or effect of concealing information about a public hazard [S2] [S3].

Voids and bars enforcement of any portion of a federal-court settlement agreement that conceals information about a public hazard, so companies could no longer buy silence with a settlement [S2] [S3].

Gives any substantially affected person — and automatically treats the news media as affected — standing to go to court to obtain disclosure of hazard information hidden by such an order or settlement [S2] [S3].

Closes two escape hatches: courts must examine disputed information privately (in camera) rather than take a party's word that it is harmless, and copyrighting hazard information cannot be used to keep it from being disclosed or used [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defendants in federal lawsuits — mainly product manufacturers and their insurers — who would lose the ability to bury adverse evidence in confidential settlements, and parties with genuine trade secrets who would face new challenges to confidentiality agreements.

drawbacks.text: Confidentiality is one reason parties settle at all; making hazard-related settlements unenforceable could push some cases to trial instead, raising litigation costs, and defendants argue that unvetted allegations could be disclosed even when meritless — the bill's in-camera court review and its narrow focus on things that 'caused damage and is likely to do so again' are the limits on that risk [S2] [S3].

Critics of such laws argue that courts can already weigh the public's interest when deciding whether to seal records, so a blanket statute risks sweeping in legitimate business secrets along with true public hazards [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real and specific: secret settlements have historically kept known product and safety dangers hidden from the next wave of buyers, and this bill directly targets that practice while leaving ordinary confidential business disputes alone through its in-camera review requirement. The cost is some added litigation and some loss of settlement privacy for defendants, which is largely the point. The bill's weakest spot is the breadth of its 'public hazard' definition, which courts would have to apply case by case.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee; the subcommittee held one hearing in September 1992 but the bill was never marked up, never reached the House floor, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Lawrence Smith of Florida introduced the bill on April 23, 1991, with eight Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on June 7, 1991 sent to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration [S5].

The committee requested executive comment from the Justice Department and the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts in July 1991, and the subcommittee held hearings on September 10, 1992 — but no further action followed [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote in either chamber and expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use confidential settlements to keep evidence of dangerous products out of public view kept that tool intact, because the bill died in committee without a vote. Litigants who prefer sealed records, and the defense bar that negotiates them, are better off than they would have been had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defendants who seal hazard evidence in settlements

for.name: Rep. Lawrence Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through introduction and referral.

for.name: Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on September 10, 1992, its only advancement beyond referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Full committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup; the bill sat for more than a year after its subcommittee hearing and never reached the House floor.

against.name: Defendants' bar and corporate litigants
against.role: Opponents of limits on confidential settlements
against.what_they_did: No opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill, but the business community historically opposed Sunshine in Litigation measures as unnecessary interference with settlement privacy; the bill's death without any floor action meant this opposition never had to prevail in a recorded vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats, but no votes were ever taken, so the record shows only the bill's partisan sponsorship and not how the chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have voided settlement clauses that hide evidence of dangers their products caused, ending a tool for keeping bad safety records out of public view. Losing that tool is the public's gain, since the same concealed documents often describe risks to future customers.

Insurers rely on confidential settlements to resolve claims cheaply and quietly; the bill would have made secrecy clauses covering hazards unenforceable, likely raising settlement and litigation costs that flow into premiums.
The bill expressly gave the press standing to sue to unseal hazard information, expanding reporters' access to court records that secrecy orders currently close.
